articles.title: DeepMind's ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03673-0AlphaGenome 2 can predict the types of cells where a DNA variant is likely to act.
articles.content:
Credit: Hiroshi Watanabe/Getty

In 2024, researchers found a new driver of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): it was a gene called ETS2 that is overactive in immune cells due to a DNA variant that predisposes people to the condition. This variant had previously confounded researchers because it lies in a ‘gene desert’ nowhere near protein-coding sequences.

That discovery had involved gene-editing and other sophisticated molecular biology techniques and identified potential new IBD treatments. Now, researchers at Google DeepMind in London have replicated aspects of the finding using an AI model, and they have done this without lifting a pipette. Their model is called AlphaGenome 2.

“They’ve managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments,” says James Lee, an immunologist and geneticist at the Francis Crick Institute in London who led the 2024 study. “It’s reassuring from our perspective.”

The AlphaGenome 2 model, which was announced today, is an update to an AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences, such as on the expression of other genes. These sequences comprise 98% of the human genome, but they are among the hardest to decipher. The latest model makes these predictions in hundreds of different mouse and human cell types.

Two months ago, Google DeepMind released the AlphaGenome Atlas: these were predictions for every possible single-letter DNA change to the human genome – a total of 9 billion different variants.

These and other predictions were made with a tool called AlphaGenome 1 and came with a major caveat: they did not specify the precise kind of cell – be it antibody-making B cells or pancreatic beta-cells – in which a variant was likely to act. “Having something that cannot predict cell type specificity is a bit of a problem, which is why it hasn’t been hugely useful for us,” says Lee.

But researchers know that many non-coding DNA sequences – including the variant that Lee’s team mapped, which is part of a sequence called a gene enhancer – tend to be active in specific types of cells.

“If you want to understand variants associated with genetic diseases, then you have to ask yourself what are the cell types that are affected,” says Žiga Avsec, a Google DeepMind researcher who leads the AlphaGenome team.

100 million cells

To develop an AI model that could decipher variant effects in diverse cells, Avsec’s team trained AlphaGenome 2 on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. AlphaGenome 1, by contrast, was fed data collected in ‘bulk’ samples of heterogeneous cells.

The result is a richer, more fine-grained representation of the differences between cells, says Adam Gayoso, a Google DeepMind scientist and co-author of a preprint describing the model on the company’s website.

The model also isn’t limited to making predictions in the 637 types of human and 311 mouse cells it was trained with. Researchers can provide the model with new single-cell gene activity data – such as cells in a disease state – and generate gene variant predictions. This could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says Gayoso.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant breakthrough in genome mapping using AI, enabling rapid and precise prediction of DNA variant effects in specific cell types. This advancement has broad implications for understanding genetic diseases and accelerating medical research, benefiting society at large. The article provides detailed context on the technology, its development, and its potential impact on health research.

articles.title: Blood-thinning drug limits cartilage damage and relieves osteoarthritis pain
articles.summary: A study in animals suggests a drug used to thin blood might eventually be able to slow down the development of osteoarthritis. Currently, there are no approved drugs capable of doing this
articles.content:
A study in animals suggests a drug used to thin blood might eventually be able to slow down the development of osteoarthritis. Currently, there are no approved drugs capable of doing this

Coloured X-ray of osteoarthritis of the knee ALAIN POL/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage.

Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease.

“We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Advertisement

It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues.

To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis.

A month later, four of the monkeys took a daily dose of a drug called dabigatran, mixed into their food. Dabigatran is commonly used to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk of strokes, but has also been shown to block inflammatory signals via both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The remaining monkeys ate their usual food as a control.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

After seven months, MRI scans revealed that the left-knee cartilage in monkeys on dabigratan was about 60 per cent thicker, on average, compared to the control monkeys. This suggests that the drug reduced cartilage damage, slowing the progression of osteoarthritis, says Liu.

Monkeys on dabigratan also had a roughly 15 per cent greater range of motion in their left knee than the control monkeys. “Monkeys receiving dabigatran showed a more natural walking pattern and a greater range of knee movement,” says Liu. “These improvements are consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.”

In further experiments, the team confirmed their findings in mice with surgically-induced knee osteoarthritis, which also revealed that dabigratan reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 per cent.

The findings suggest dabigratan could slow the progression of osteoarthritis in people. “They’ve used the best [animal] models we have of osteoarthritis,” says Vincent. “If the findings can be replicated by another research group, you would certainly consider trying a small clinical trial,” she says.

But it is unclear whether the approach can reverse damage that has already occurred, says Liu. Another limitation is that giving people a drug that reduces blood clotting puts them at greater risk of bleeds, so the researchers are now developing drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without reducing clotting, which they will test in mice before any clinical trials, says Liu.

However, Vincent says prior studies suggest that inhibiting molecules involved in blood clotting may relieve osteoarthritis symptoms, which might mean that some of dabigratan’s benefits are due to its anti-clotting, rather than anti-inflammatory, effect. Further research that compares dabigatran with drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without the clotting effects should help to clarify this, she says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery where a blood-thinning drug shows potential to slow osteoarthritis progression, a condition affecting over 500 million people globally. The study demonstrates measurable benefits in animal models, including reduced cartilage damage and improved mobility, addressing a major unmet medical need with no current approved disease-modifying treatments. The research is detailed, focused, and suggests a promising new therapeutic avenue with broad public health implications.

articles.personality_presentation:

articles.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
articles.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.
articles.content:
Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery using ancient protein analysis to reveal new insights into the social behavior and biology of an extinct human relative, Homo naledi. This breakthrough has broad implications for understanding human evolution and ancient social customs, offering a meaningful and inspiring advancement in paleoanthropology with tangible benefits for scientific knowledge.

articles.personality_title_es: Dientes antiguos revelan posible sitio de entierro solo para hembras de Homo naledi
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Científicos han estudiado fósiles de Homo naledi, un pariente humano extinto que vivió en Sudáfrica hace entre 240,000 y 335,000 años. Estos fósiles se encontraron en la cueva Rising Star, donde los investigadores notaron algo extraño: los huesos de los adultos eran muy similares, con poca diferencia entre machos y hembras.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo internacional analizó proteínas preservadas en el esmalte dental de al menos 20 individuos de Homo naledi. Buscaron una proteína específica de los machos llamada Amelogenina-Y, vinculada al cromosoma Y. Sorprendentemente, no encontraron señales de esta proteína, lo que sugiere que todos los fósiles podrían pertenecer a hembras. Este descubrimiento se publicó en la revista Cell.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque podría significar que la cueva fue usada como un lugar de entierro especial solo para hembras, mostrando evidencia temprana de costumbres sociales como entierros selectivos. Se pensaba que este comportamiento era exclusivo de los humanos modernos. Otra explicación es que la proteína masculina faltara debido a cambios genéticos en Homo naledi. De cualquier manera, el estudio muestra cómo las proteínas antiguas en los dientes pueden revelar detalles nuevos sobre humanos extintos más allá de los huesos.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando los fósiles y la cueva para entender mejor la vida social de Homo naledi. También planean usar análisis de proteínas en otros fósiles antiguos para aprender más sobre los primeros humanos y sus formas de vida.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los científicos no encontraron proteínas masculinas en los dientes antiguos de Homo naledi, lo que sugiere que la cueva Rising Star podría haber sido un sitio de entierro solo para hembras o que esta especie tenía una genética única.

articles.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.
articles.content:
Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals."

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals."

This breakthrough enhances understanding of biological development with broad implications for biology and medicine, potentially impacting future research in tissue engineering and regenerative health. Au lieu d’avoir besoin d’instructions compliquées, le modèle montre que de simples mouvements cellulaires en réponse aux signaux chimiques peuvent expliquer l’apparition et l’organisation des follicules.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren un proceso simple detrás de los patrones de crecimiento del pelo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Antes de que nazca un mamífero, su piel comienza a decidir dónde crecerá el pelo formando puntos especiales llamados folículos pilosos. Estos puntos forman patrones que varían según la especie. Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos han preguntado cómo el cuerpo crea estos patrones ordenados y complejos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Ginebra estudiaron cómo las células se mueven al seguir señales químicas. Crearon un modelo por computadora que mostró cómo se forman los patrones de folículos en ratones y ratones espinosos. En lugar de necesitar instrucciones complicadas, el modelo mostró que simples movimientos celulares en respuesta a señales químicas pueden explicar cómo aparecen y se organizan los folículos.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento desafía una teoría antigua que decía que un nuevo folículo impide que otros crezcan cerca usando químicos. También muestra que los diferentes patrones de pelo o escamas en animales pueden venir del mismo proceso básico, solo que con variaciones en cómo reaccionan las células o crece la piel. Esto ayuda a entender mejor cómo la naturaleza crea diseños complejos sin un plan detallado.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo podría investigar cómo funciona este proceso simple en otros animales y tejidos. Esto podría ayudar en la medicina, como en la ingeniería de tejidos, donde se intenta crecer o reparar piel y pelo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un proceso sencillo donde las células siguen señales químicas puede explicar cómo los animales desarrollan sus patrones únicos de pelo sin instrucciones complejas.
